title: Bhagat Singh
hook: born into a Sikh family, the young revolutionary later wrote of doubting God, and is honored across Punjab

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udham Singh, and your line was a long memory. Did an older person tell you something the family had forgotten? Today, a young man whose face is painted on walls across Punjab. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

On a truck's back panel, on a college wall, on a sticker on a scooter: the same young face, a mustache, sometimes a turban, sometimes a hat tilted to one side. Ask the driver who it is and you'll get two words, said with real pride. Bhagat Singh. Ask what he believed about God, and the answer gets more interesting. He was born into a Sikh family. And near the end of his short life, in a prison cell, he sat down and wrote out, as carefully as he could, why he no longer believed.
screen: `THE SAME FACE ON TRUCKS AND WALLS.` → `TURBAN OR HAT.` → `A PRISON CELL, AND A PEN.`

segments.voice: First, the family. Bhagat Singh grew up in a Sikh household in Punjab, in a family already caught up in the struggle against British rule. Second, the revolutionary. As a young man he turned to armed struggle against the British, and that path ended in a trial in Lahore. He was hanged there, together with two companions, Sukhdev and Rajguru. Third, the essay. While waiting in prison, he wrote a piece titled Why I Am an Atheist. In it he explains, plainly and without mockery, how he came to doubt God, and he insists that he arrived there by thinking it through, not out of pride. He writes, too, that he expects to face the gallows without turning to belief for comfort at the end. Fourth, the honor. Bhagat Singh is honored across Punjab and beyond by religious and non-religious people alike. Some Sikhs who pray every morning keep his picture on the wall. Those who share his doubt claim him too. Nobody needs to settle his beliefs to honor his courage and his candor. And Guru Nanak gives the Sikh measure of a life, at Ang 62 of the Guru Granth Sahib: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Bhagat Singh's conclusions about God are his own, and Sikh teaching does not share them. What his admirers point to is that he didn't pretend. He said what he thought, and he lived it to the end. That's today's line.
screen: `A SIKH HOUSEHOLD IN PUNJAB.` · `ARMED STRUGGLE, A TRIAL, THE GALLOWS.` · `WHY I AM AN ATHEIST.` · `HIGHER STILL IS TRUTHFUL LIVING.` · then, large: `AN HONEST MIND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for an honest doubter. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone who doesn't believe what you believe, or who believes nothing at all, and who has told you so honestly. Picture their face as they said it. Notice any urge to argue, and let it pass on the next breath out. Then find one thing to respect in them: their honesty, their care, the way they thought it through. Hold that for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhagat Singh. A young revolutionary from a Sikh family, hanged in Lahore, who wrote in prison of why he doubted God, and is honored across Punjab. Today's word.
Your line: an honest mind. Today, when someone tells you plainly what they think, even if you disagree, thank them for saying it straight. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Bhagat Singh is remembered across Punjab, by Sikhs and by others, as a shaheed of the freedom struggle; his picture hangs in homes and shops, and his anniversary is marked with gatherings.
